description: Sabotages for win-numa-sys's buffer-trait implementations (IB-1.2). Run with tools/run-sabotage.ps1; see tools/README-sabotage.md for the format and for why the results are read the way they are.
notCoveredHere: The allocator itself (buffer.rs) and the node queries (node.rs) have no entries here: this manifest was added with the buffer-trait implementations, and covers only them. Whether the pages landed on the node asked for is not observable on the single-node host these tests run on, as buffer/tests.rs says.

sabotages.name: IB-1.2: the shared address is null
sabotages.why: A null address is the one a ring would hand the kernel. Compared against the buffer's own pointer, and read back after a write through the mutable one, so a plausible wrong pointer fails too. Scored as a process abort, because the test that reads through the pointer builds a slice from it and Rust's precondition check aborts on a null one; the correspondence test fails an assertion on its own, which is the deterministic catch, and the abort only hides it.

sabotages.name: IB-1.2: the length reported is the mapped one, not the requested one
sabotages.why: The allocation is page-granular. Reporting the page-rounded length tells the kernel it may use bytes the caller never asked about.

sabotages.name: IB-1.2: the mutable address is null
sabotages.why: The mutable trait's obligation is that its address equals the shared one, so the kernel writes where the owner reads. Scored as a process abort for the reason the first entry gives; the correspondence test fails an assertion on its own.

sabotages.name: CONTROL: the address is read through the type rather than the method
sabotages.why: The manifest checking itself: NumaBuffer::as_ptr(self) is the same call spelled differently, on code every test runs. If it comes back caught, something is reacting to text rather than behaviour.
